text: christ pantocrator christ almighty pantokrator christ christ pantocrator presents christ as the almighty. thomas hopko’s explanation of church imagery places christ the almighty at the centre of the building, within a wider programme of images of the church and kingdom. the displayed sinai icon shows christ facing the viewer, with a cross-marked halo, a hand raised in blessing, and a richly covered gospel book. it is a single frontal portrait rather than a narrative scene. the image catalogue identifies this as the sixth-century encaustic christ pantocrator of saint catherine’s monastery at sinai. its material and date belong to this particular surviving work, rather than to every later icon bearing the same title. hopko connects the possibility of depicting christ with the incarnation: the word truly became human. his catechesis treats icons as witnesses to god’s presence and the kingdom, with john 1:14 among its explicit scriptural foundations. and the word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the father,) full of grace and truth.

the savior not made by hands holy mandylion holy napkin acheiropoietos christ the savior not made by hands is associated with the holy mandylion, the cloth bearing christ’s face in the church’s account of abgar of edessa. the oca commemorates its translation to constantinople on august 16. the example is simon ushakov’s historical depiction of christ’s face upon a suspended cloth. it represents the received mandylion subject; the painted panel itself is an artist’s work, not the cloth described in the traditional account. the oca relates that the ill ruler abgar sought christ’s help and that christ imprinted his face on a cloth sent to edessa. the same account dates the transfer to constantinople to 944. these are identified as the published church narrative and its dated commemoration. metropolitan tikhon explains the feast on two levels: the particular mandylion and christ himself as the true image of the father who freely became human. who is the image of the invisible god, the firstborn of every creature: for by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him: and he is before all things, and by him all things consist.

christ enthroned savior on the throne christ christ enthroned depicts christ in royal glory. hopko’s account of the iconostasis relates the glorified christ to his coming as king and judge, while also identifying enthroned christ as one traditional image behind the altar. this medieval example depicts christ seated centrally, blessing with one hand and holding a book with the other. smaller sacred figures surround the throne and occupy the border. the file catalogue names the work savior on the throne, with a selection of saints. the selected reproduction identifies the icon as a thirteenth-century work photographed at the tretyakov gallery. that attribution concerns the displayed example; the general subject also occurs in other centuries and church settings. hopko places such images within the church’s proclamation of the kingdom. his description offers several possible altar images of christ in glory, including enthroned, transfigured and risen representations. and immediately i was in the spirit: and, behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one sat on the throne. and he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.

christ emmanuel christ immanuel savior emmanuel christ christ emmanuel represents christ as a child or young person. basilica’s explanation links the title with isaiah’s prophecy and matthew’s interpretation of emmanuel as god with us, rather than limiting the image to a particular episode of infancy. the displayed russian icon presents the youthful face of christ within a halo. the object is catalogued at the national museum of tatarstan as an eighteenth-century work in tempera on a prepared wooden panel; the photograph carries its own creative commons licence. this catalogue date identifies the particular russian panel. it should be distinguished from the much earlier scriptural name emmanuel and from other representations of the child christ, including nativity scenes and images with his mother. basilica interprets the combination of youthful appearance, mature facial features and a high forehead as expressing both christ’s human life and divine wisdom. the article explicitly relates the composition to isaiah 7:14 and matthew 1:23. now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the lord by the prophet, saying, behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name emmanuel, which being interpreted is, god with us.

christ the bridegroom the bridegroom ho nymphios christ the bridegroom is the title used in the holy week services of the first three days. goarch relates it to the bridegroom in the parable of the ten virgins and to christ’s passion and second coming. goarch describes the icon as christ during his mockery by soldiers: crowned with thorns, clothed in purple and holding a reed. this is the humiliated king during the passion, with the gospel’s royal title turned into the soldiers’ taunt. the pictured historical greek icon is identified as christ the bridegroom from saint paraskevi church in langadas. its surviving painted surface visibly includes the thorn-crowned christ and the identifying greek title; losses in the paint have not been reconstructed. the archdiocesan explanation associates the bridegroom imagery with the union of christ and the church and the expectation of his return. the evening services from palm sunday through holy tuesday are the orthros of the following day. and at midnight there was a cry made, behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him. then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.

christ: extreme humility man of sorrows akra tapeinosis christ extreme humility is represented here by a historical man of sorrows icon. the byzantine and christian museum describes this iconographic theme through the dead christ standing within the sarcophagus, rather than through a scene of the soldiers mocking him. in the museum’s account of nikolaos tzafouris’s example, christ wears a loincloth and crosses his hands low on the body. the museum calls it a simple version of a byzantine composition that can also include the virgin and john the evangelist. the displayed image is catalogued as a man of sorrows by nikolaos tzafouris. it shows christ’s closed eyes, wounds and crossed hands above the tomb. the reproduction retains the historical panel’s worn surface and painted frame. the museum places the wider composition’s popularity between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. its catalogue describes the type; that description is not a new instruction for prayer or a claim that every variant has identical details. but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.

christ anapeson reclining christ anapeson christ this entry shows christ anapeson, the reclining christ, in the dionysiou monastery fresco. the catalogue identifies a sixteenth-century work on mount athos. the title is kept distinct here from every later russian composition called the unsleeping eye. christ reclines as a child in the centre, attended by the mother of god and an angelic figure. the displayed composition belongs to the fresco identified by its source as anapeson at dionysiou, rather than an illustration of a particular gospel verse. the file metadata attributes the fresco to tzortzis phouka and dates it to 1547. these catalogue details refer to this particular work. they do not establish the date of origin of all reclining-christ imagery. archpriest david lesko discusses a related russian unsleeping eye composition as an image of christ’s protective vigilance, first appearing there around the end of the fifteenth century. he connects its symbolism with the lion of judah, but explicitly distinguishes the slumber of the christ child from the unsleeping eye in footnote 2. these titles therefore cannot be treated as exact synonyms for all variants. judah is a lion’s whelp: from the prey, my son, thou art gone up: he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as an old lion; who shall rouse him up?

the hospitality of abraham: holy trinity rublev’s trinity old testament trinity hospitality of abraham scriptural scenes rublev’s holy trinity draws on the visit to abraham in genesis 18. natalya sheredega’s museum article explains the history of interpreting the three visitors and the particular concentration of rublev’s composition on their unity. three winged figures sit around a table with a cup. a building, a tree and a mountain form the background. the catalogue contrasts this concentrated composition with more detailed hospitality scenes that include abraham and sarah serving their guests. sheredega identifies the artist as andrei rublev and the place of creation as trinity–saint sergius monastery. her article records disagreement over the precise date: proposed settings include the wooden cathedral of 1411 and the later stone cathedral’s decoration in 1425–27. the article distinguishes several older interpretations of abraham’s visitors, including god with two angels and a symbolic manifestation of the trinity. it presents rublev’s image within the latter tradition, rather than treating every interpretation of genesis 18 as identical. and the lord appeared unto him in the plains of mamre: and he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day; and he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him: and when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself toward the ground,

the vladimir icon of the mother of god our lady of vladimir vladimirskaya tenderness theotokos the vladimir icon presents the mother of god and christ with their faces touching. the displayed historical image is the widely reproduced vladimir work, rather than an interchangeable portrait of mary or a generic image of mother and child. christ reaches around his mother’s neck while she inclines her face toward him. the worn historical painted surface is visible. the source identifies the work as the virgin of vladimir; the reproduction is retained without restoration or added details. the oca’s account attributes the prototype to saint luke within church tradition. it records the icon’s arrival from constantinople in 1131, its transfer to vladimir in 1155 and its first arrival in moscow in 1395. traditional authorship should be distinguished from the surviving object’s art-historical identification. the august 26 commemoration concerns the meeting of the icon in moscow. the oca connects it with the city’s deliverance from tamerlane and relates a vision of the mother of god as part of that church narrative. and mary said, my soul doth magnify the lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in god my saviour. for he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed. for he that is mighty hath done to me great things; and holy is his name.

the kazan icon of the mother of god our lady of kazan kazanskaya theotokos the kazan icon is especially venerated in the russian church, with important examples associated with kazan, saint petersburg and moscow. the oca’s july 8 account relates its discovery and the subsequent veneration of multiple copies. the pictured panel is a mid-nineteenth-century kazan icon, with smaller saints on the borders. mary inclines her head beside the upright christ child. this later example is identified separately from the icon whose discovery is narrated for 1579. the published church account places the discovery after a destructive fire in kazan in 1579. nine-year-old matrona reported repeated visions indicating the location. the account names the priest ermogenes, later patriarch, as a witness who wrote about the finding. the oca relates healings of blind people during the icon’s first procession and explains the prominence of its veneration. these reported miracles belong to the source’s church narrative. the many later copies should not all be called the same original physical object. and it came to pass, that, when elisabeth heard the salutation of mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and elisabeth was filled with the holy ghost: and she spake out with a loud voice, and said, blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb. and whence is this to me, that the mother of my lord should come to me?

the iveron icon of the mother of god iviron iverian portaitissa gate-keeper theotokos the iveron icon is associated with iviron monastery on mount athos. the oca explains its greek title portaitissa as gate-keeper, connecting the name with the icon’s repeated appearance at the monastery’s entrance in the traditional account. the displayed iveron image shows mary holding christ and gesturing toward him, with their faces and hands visible through a decorated metal covering. it is identified by its file source as the iveron image, not as an unrelated marian portrait. the church narrative begins with a widow near nicaea during emperor theophilos’s iconoclasm. after a soldier wounds the image, she commits it to the sea. the oca then relates how the georgian monk gabriel receives it from the water at mount athos. these miraculous events are presented as received church tradition. the source associates the icon’s place at the gate with the mother of god’s protection of the community. its explanation of the title concerns that particular narrative, while the image itself directs attention to mary and her son. and when they wanted wine, the mother of jesus saith unto him, they have no wine. jesus saith unto her, woman, what have i to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come. his mother saith unto the servants, whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.

the tikhvin icon of the mother of god our lady of tikhvin tikhvinskaya theotokos the tikhvin icon belongs to the hodegetria family of mother-and-child images. archpriest john matusiak’s account combines its russian monastic history, accounts of miracles and its twentieth-century preservation outside russia. matusiak identifies a distinguishing detail: the christ child’s legs are crossed and the sole of a foot faces the viewer. the virgin’s pose relates it to hodegetria images such as the iveron icon, while the child’s feet help distinguish this particular composition. the source explicitly labels the attribution to saint luke as ancient tradition. it relates an appearance above lake ladoga in 1383 and the icon’s settling near tikhvin. during the second world war it was taken from the monastery; bishop john garklavs brought it to the united states in 1949. the account links the icon with the protection of the monastery during swedish attacks in 1613–14 and with later venerated copies. it reports that the 2003 pilgrimage began its journey back to russia; that passage describes the journey at its beginning. and he went down with them, and came to nazareth, and was subject unto them: but his mother kept all these sayings in her heart. and jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with god and man.

the smolensk icon of the mother of god smolensk hodegetria hodegetria directress theotokos the oca translates hodegetria as she who leads the way. its account identifies the smolensk icon with a particular history of transfer, veneration and later copies; the iconographic title also applies to a wider family of images. the pictured example is dionysius’s hodegetria, catalogued as a work of 1482 in the russian museum. mary holds christ and extends her hand toward him. this specific later painted example is distinguished from the earlier icon described in the smolensk tradition. the oca presents the attribution to saint luke as church tradition. it describes the byzantine princess anna bringing the icon when she married prince vsevolod in 1046, and vladimir monomachos subsequently placing it in smolensk’s dormition cathedral at the beginning of the twelfth century. the account distinguishes an ancient image and later copies, including those associated with the events of 1812. july 28 commemorates the smolensk icon and its venerated copies; the source also records a separate november 5 observance. jesus saith unto him, i am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the father, but by me. if ye had known me, ye should have known my father also: and from henceforth ye know him, and have seen him.

the kursk root icon of the mother of god kursk root kursk-root our lady of the sign of kursk theotokos the kursk root icon is a particular image of the mother of god of the sign, closely associated with rocor. the synod’s history relates its name to its discovery beside a tree root in the kursk region. the mother of god appears in prayer with christ before her; the surrounding figures are old testament prophets. the synod dates the addition of the prophetic surround to 1597, when tsar feodor ioannovich ordered the icon brought to moscow. the synod’s narrative dates the hunter’s discovery to 1295 and relates a spring appearing when he lifts the icon. it also recounts the image’s being cut in two during an attack in 1383 and miraculously reuniting after the priest’s return. these are the source’s received accounts. the account records its departure from russia in 1920 and placement in belgrade in 1925. it identifies the icon with the life of the russian church abroad and notes that saint john of shanghai and san francisco died before it in 1966. therefore the lord himself shall give you a sign; behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name immanuel.

the don icon of the mother of god our lady of the don donskaya theotokos the don icon presents the mother of god and christ in a close embrace, their faces touching. the selected historical reproduction is the work traditionally associated with theophanes the greek, not an unrelated icon of the same saintly subjects. the child turns toward mary and raises an arm around her neck; his uncovered legs and feet are visible. mary inclines her head while supporting him. the painted panel’s gold ground and worn surface remain visible in the reproduction. the oca attributes the icon to theophanes the greek and connects it with the battle of kulikovo in 1380. in the church account, the don cossacks give it to prince demetrius after the victory, and he brings it to moscow. these associations are presented as the published ecclesiastical account. the same account relates the icon’s use during the threat to moscow in 1591 and the founding of the don monastery in thanksgiving in 1592. it records august 19 as the icon’s feast, linking the commemoration to the city’s deliverance. and simeon blessed them, and said unto mary his mother, behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in israel; and for a sign which shall be spoken against; (yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,) that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.

the pochaev icon of the mother of god our lady of pochaev pochayiv theotokos the pochaev icon is associated with the dormition monastery in southwest ukraine. father alexander golubov’s historical account distinguishes written evidence about the monastery and the icon’s donation from local traditions concerning earlier apparitions. golubov describes mary holding christ on her right arm and a cloth covering his feet. the child blesses; seven smaller saints appear along the sides and bottom. the displayed image shows the decorated shrine around this particular mother-and-child composition. his account connects the icon with metropolitan neophyte’s visit in 1559 and his gift to anna goiskaya. anna’s 1597 endowment transferred the icon to the monastery. a distinct local tradition places an apparition and footprint at mount pochaev around 1340. the oca’s july 23 commemoration concerns deliverance from the siege of 1675. its narrative describes the mother of god and saint job appearing above the monastery. it also identifies monastery books as records of reported healings and other miracles. for he that is mighty hath done to me great things; and holy is his name. and his mercy is on them that fear him from generation to generation.

the mother of god of the sign our lady of the sign znamenie novgorod sign theotokos the mother of god of the sign is an iconographic type and also the title of particular venerated icons. the oca’s november 27 entry treats the novgorod icon and then distinguishes other local examples, including kursk. mary is depicted with raised hands, while the child christ appears before her breast within a mandorla. the oca describes this circular or oval enclosure as a defining feature. the novgorod example displayed here is one historical realization of the type. the source dates the type’s appearance in russia to the eleventh and twelfth centuries. its novgorod narrative concerns the siege of 1170: an arrow strikes the icon during a procession, tears appear, and the attackers are overcome. this is the church’s account of the commemoration. the same entry records an observance instituted in memory of the deliverance and describes the spread of venerated copies with local names, including the kursk and abalaka images. these are particular local icons sharing the sign composition. rocor’s explanation connects the sign composition to isaiah 7:14, the prophecy of the virgin and emmanuel. that scriptural reference does not assign every later panel the same physical history. therefore the lord himself shall give you a sign; behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name immanuel.

the mother of god: quick to hear quick to hearken gorgoepikoos skoroposlushnitsa theotokos the oca places the venerated quick to hear image at dokheiariou monastery on mount athos. its account connects the name with the repentance of the monk neilos and a promise that the mother of god would hear those who approached her. the athonite image is a fresco beside the entrance to the monastery refectory, on its eastern exterior wall. the source distinguishes this original location from the later chapel and from painted copies carried to other orthodox communities. according to the monastery narrative published by the oca, neilos repeatedly passed the image with a smoking torch in 1664. he disregarded a warning, lost his sight, and remained before the icon asking forgiveness. the account describes his sight returning and the subsequent enclosure of the corridor as a chapel. a copy made on athos was sent to archbishop tikhon and brought to saint tikhon’s monastery in pennsylvania in may 1906. the published explanation presents the title through intercession and forgiveness. it also describes the prosmonarios, the monk appointed to care for the chapel and lamps. these are details of the monastery’s established devotion, rather than a new prayer rule for readers.

the mother of god: softener of evil hearts softening of evil hearts simeon’s prophecy theotokos this image is associated with simeon’s prophecy to mary in luke 2:35. the orthodox word explains its seven swords as the fullness of her sorrow, especially in witnessing christ’s suffering and crucifixion. the date when the type first appeared is unknown. the mother of god is shown without the infant christ, with three swords on each side and one below. the oca distinguishes this arrangement from seven arrows, whose seven weapons are grouped four on one side and three on the other. the orthodox word separately describes the contemporary travelling image associated with bachurino. it is a manufactured sofrino print mounted on wood, not an ancient original. the article relates that it began streaming myrrh after being placed on saint matrona’s reliquary in 1999; it later travelled with its guardian sergei fomin. the historical reproduction shown here represents the iconographic type and is distinct from that modern travelling print. the article places the imagery within mary’s suffering at her son’s passion. its explanation of the number seven is explicitly the publication’s theological interpretation. (yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,) that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.

the mother of god: unexpected joy nechayannaya radost theotokos the oca connects unexpected joy with a story recorded by saint demetrius of rostov in the fleece of prayer. the joy in this narrative is the forgiveness received by a repentant sinner. its printed principal commemoration is december 9. the composition contains an icon within the icon: a youth kneels in a room before an image of the mother of god and christ. wounds appear on the child’s hands, feet, and side as the narrative unfolds. in the published account, the young man has a devotion to the theotokos while continuing to plan sinful acts. one day, before going out to sin, he sees blood flowing from christ’s wounds. he asks who has caused them and hears that he and other sinners crucify her son again. the encounter brings recognition of his conduct and prolonged, tearful repentance. the story ends with mercy and forgiveness, rather than merely with his surprise at a miraculous sight. the oca also prints january 25 and may 1 as commemorations. its reference to judges 6:36–40 identifies the scriptural fleece associated with the book’s title; that passage is not the biblical narration of this later icon story.

the mother of god: inexhaustible chalice inexhaustible cup neupivaemaya chasha theotokos the oca identifies the inexhaustible chalice as an orans image and links its veneration with serpukhov and a retired soldier’s recovery from destructive drinking. its account differentiates the original, whose later whereabouts are unknown, from subsequent copies. the mother of god raises her hands in prayer. before her, the christ child stands in a chalice. the source explicitly identifies this as the communion chalice, rather than interpreting the vessel as an ordinary drinking cup. the church narrative places the soldier in tula province in 1878. repeated dreams direct him to a monastery at serpukhov. the nuns initially do not recognize the requested icon, then find its name inscribed on the reverse. he recognizes saint barlaam of serpukhov as the elder from his dream. the oca recounts the soldier’s deliverance, the closure of the monastery in 1919, and the revival of veneration through copies made in 1993 and 1995. the published meaning emphasizes consolation, mercy, and repentance. the entry says the precise day of the icon’s revelation is unknown; it records the church-wide celebration on may 5 established in 1997 in connection with saint barlaam’s commemoration.

the mother of god: joy of all who sorrow joy of all who sorrow theotokos joy of all who sorrow is a family of images portraying the mother of god amid people in distress. the oca’s october 24 account explains the composition and recounts the healing associated with the moscow image in 1688. mary appears full length, surrounded by people who are hungry, unclothed, oppressed, or otherwise suffering. angels attend them and direct attention toward her. the oca notes variants with christ in her arms and variants without the child, as well as differences in her garments. the moscow account concerns euphemia, the sister of patriarch joachim, who suffered from a severe wound. in the narrative, a voice directs her to an image in the transfiguration church on ordynka. after the icon is brought and a service held, her healing on october 24, 1688 becomes the occasion for its feast. the same entry distinguishes the later petersburg image associated with coins, rather than treating every image bearing this title as one physical object. the oca interprets the title as consolation in suffering and describes the theotokos as interceding for those in need. its explanation links the surrounding figures to the subject of the icon and to the care offered to the suffering.

the mother of god: sweet kissing glykophilousa sweet kiss theotokos sweet kissing names a tender mother-and-child composition. the oca describes the particular venerated glykophilousa at philotheou monastery on mount athos. the artwork shown here is a historical example of the type, not a claim to be the philotheou original. the mother of god inclines toward christ as he embraces her. the oca places this composition within the eleousa, or virgin of tenderness, category and remarks on the unusually close embrace and affectionate expression of the philotheou image. according to the tradition recounted by the oca, victoria preserved an icon from her iconoclast husband during the reign of theophilos by casting it into the sea. it arrived at athos, where the monks of philotheou received it. the account associates a spring with the landing place and records a bright monday procession. it locates the venerated image on a pillar at the left of the monastery’s main church and gives march 27 and bright monday as its commemorations. the source presents the affection exchanged by christ and his mother as the characteristic of this type. the rescue-at-sea account belongs to philotheou’s sacred tradition; another historical glykophilousa image need not share that object’s individual provenance.

the mother of god: hodegetria hodegetria hodegetria the guide theotokos hodegetria is a mother-and-child type in which mary indicates christ. the oca relates the name and the venerated constantinopolitan image to the monastery of the guides. the type is represented by numerous later icons, rather than one surviving original. in the oca’s description, the theotokos holds christ with her left arm and indicates him with her right hand. the meaning of the pointing gesture is given through christ’s identification of himself as the way, truth, and life in john 14:6. the entry records the church tradition that saint luke painted an image of mary from life and received her blessing. this is a traditional attribution, rather than independently established authorship for the artwork displayed here. the account follows the sacred image from palestine to constantinople through empress eudokia and saint pulcheria, and says it was destroyed when constantinople fell in 1453. it names a copy at xenophontos monastery on athos. the published explanation makes the gesture christ-directed: mary indicates the way leading to her son. its biblical reference supplies the interpretation; the profile does not infer a new message from the background ornament or the colors of this particular reproduction.

the mother of god: orans virgin orans oranta praying mother of god theotokos orans means praying in latin. in a report published by the romanian patriarchate’s basilica agency, patriarch daniel explains the extended-arm image of the mother of god as an image of the church in prayer. it is a type, not a single named object. the defining gesture is mary’s outstretched arms in prayer. the patriarch’s explanation also addresses a form with christ depicted on her chest. the kyiv mosaic reproduced here shows the raised-arm figure without that additional image; the source’s account is therefore broader than this one example. one named example discussed by the oca is the mirozh icon. its account identifies the praying type, describes saints dovmont-timothy and martha beside mary, and records a copy retained at the monastery after the venerated icon was removed. those pskov details concern mirozh and must not be transferred to the kyiv mosaic. patriarch daniel connects the image with the church receiving christ’s blessing and living through it. his remarks were published when the romanian holy synod established the order of the praying theotokos in 2022, providing a modern official explanation of the image’s ecclesial meaning.

the mother of god: milk giver galaktotrophousa mlekopitatelnitsa typikonissa theotokos the oca’s milk-giver account follows a venerated image from the lavra of saint savva near jerusalem to saint savva of serbia and the athonite cell at karyes connected with hilandar. the source prints january 12 as its commemoration. the type depicts mary nursing the infant christ. the uffizi’s collection entry identifies the nursing mother of god as milk-giver; this title describes the composition rather than establishing that every image of it is the particular icon preserved at karyes. according to the tradition published by the oca, saint savva the sanctified foretold that a royal pilgrim with his own name would visit the lavra and should receive the icon. when saint savva of serbia visited in the thirteenth century, the founder’s staff fell at his feet. the monks gave him the staff, the milk-giver, and the three hands image. he took the icon to athos and placed it to the right of the iconostasis in the karyes cell church. the oca explains the additional title typikonissa by the preservation of saint savva’s rule, or typikon, at the cell. john’s statement about the word becoming flesh is presented below as scripture, in the identified kjv edition. and the word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the father,) full of grace and truth.

the protection of the mother of god pokrov intercession of the mother of god holy protection theotokos the protection icon concerns the mother of god praying for the people. the oca’s october 1 account locates the vision behind the feast in the blachernae church at constantinople and identifies saint andrew the fool-for-christ and his disciple epiphanius as its witnesses. mary extends her protecting veil over the faithful. the oca describes john the baptist and john the theologian accompanying her, and reports an early icon showing andrew contemplating the praying mother of god. individual later compositions arrange the witnesses and assembly in different ways. in the published tradition, andrew sees the theotokos during an all-night vigil in the mid-tenth century. she prays, then spreads her veil over those gathered. he asks epiphanius whether he too sees her, and his disciple confirms it. the account follows the spread of this memory in russia, including churches dedicated to the protection and the establishment of the feast associated with prince andrew bogoliubsky. the source presents the veil through the theotokos’s intercession before her son. it relates that the veil disappears when she departs, while the grace of her presence remains. the feast’s imagery is read with this vision; the same article notes chronological difficulties in identifying it with a particular raid.

the mother of god: life-giving spring life-giving fountain zoodochos pege life-giving source theotokos the life-giving spring is associated with a sanctuary of the mother of god at constantinople. the oca remembers it on bright friday and separately notes an icon commemoration on april 4. these labels are retained without a guessed civil-calendar conversion. the museum of russian art’s description of the type places mary above flowing water, surrounded by people seeking relief. its exhibition distinguishes the central image from narrative scenes around the border. the displayed historical icon is one example of this subject. the oca recounts that, before becoming emperor, leo met a thirsty blind man and heard instructions leading him to a spring. the narrative associates the man’s restored sight and leo’s later accession with the mother of god. leo then built a church there. the source traces destruction and rebuilding after constantinople’s fall, a new church consecrated in 1835, and further destruction in 1955. in this published account, the name derives from the spring and the healings associated with it. the water, sanctuary, and intercession belong to one local sacred tradition. the museum description documents the visual arrangement; the oca narrative supplies the church account of its history and veneration.

the nativity of the mother of god birth of the mother of god feasts the nativity of the theotokos celebrates mary’s birth to joachim and anna. thomas hopko’s oca explanation places the feast on september 8 and explicitly distinguishes its traditional narrative from the biblical record: mary’s birth is not narrated in the new testament. anna reclines after childbirth; the infant mary, joachim, and attendants appear around her. more elaborate compositions add joachim’s prayer and the parents’ embrace. hopko describes joachim and anna as an elderly, childless couple awaiting the messiah. in the traditional account, their prayer for a child is answered by mary’s birth. he states that the story comes from apocryphal writings outside the new testament and explains the feast as the preparation of the person who will become christ’s mother. the source’s theological account is distinguished from independent historical verification of each narrative detail. hopko connects the feast with mary’s magnificat, philippians 2:5–11, and luke 11:27–28. his explanation celebrates god’s gracious action in christ and includes the blessing of those who hear and keep god’s word. the infant in this icon is mary; it is distinct from the nativity of christ.

the entrance of the mother of god into the temple entry into the temple presentation of mary feasts the entrance concerns mary as a child entering the jerusalem temple. hopko’s oca explanation gives november 21 and identifies the narrative as church tradition without direct biblical or historical documentation. it should be distinguished from the february feast of christ’s presentation. the young mary approaches zacharias, with joachim and anna behind her. maidens carry candles; an additional scene may depict her receiving food from an angel. the traditional account describes her parents bringing mary to be raised in service to god, her welcome by zacharias, and her nourishment by angels. hopko identifies the child’s entry as preparing the living sanctuary of the divine child. his explanation draws attention to the liturgical use of old testament temple passages and mary’s magnificat, rather than treating the story as a passage omitted from the canonical gospels. the published meaning centers on mary herself becoming the dwelling place of god. hopko relates this to the new testament description of god dwelling with human beings and the church as a spiritual house. the imagery connects the temple with the incarnation; it is not an instruction for reenacting the child’s entry.

the annunciation evangelismos good tidings feasts the annunciation depicts gabriel’s announcement to mary in nazareth that she will bear jesus. hopko’s explanation places the feast on march 25, nine months before the nativity, and identifies luke 1:26–38 as the biblical account. gabriel approaches mary, who may sit or stand near a throne-like seat. some compositions show her spinning; the messenger carries a staff or scroll. the account includes gabriel’s greeting, mary’s question, the announcement of the holy spirit’s action, and her assent. hopko notes that the feast’s matins canon takes the form of dialogue between gabriel and mary. he describes the date’s frequent occurrence within great lent and the resulting variations in its services. the calendar placement concerns the church’s celebration, while the icon’s subject is the gospel encounter itself. hopko explains the feast through the good news of salvation and mary becoming the mother of god in the flesh. her response is given below directly from luke, rather than paraphrased as a new devotional instruction. and mary said, behold the handmaid of the lord; be it unto me according to thy word. and the angel departed from her.

the nativity of christ birth of christ christmas feasts this icon concerns the birth in the flesh of jesus christ. hopko explains the feast as the son of god becoming human while remaining eternally divine with the father and the holy spirit. the church’s feast is kept on december 25. mary and the swaddled infant occupy the center, with a cave, manger, angels, shepherds, magi, and joseph. some compositions include midwives bathing the child. hopko describes a forty-day preparation and a celebration patterned after the lord’s resurrection. he explains that nativity was once celebrated together with epiphany before receiving its separate date. the services draw together isaiah’s prophecies, the angelic praise from luke, matthew’s account of the magi, and paul’s teaching that god sent his son. these are readings from distinct biblical contexts; the icon brings several parts of the narrative into one composition. the published explanation makes the subject more than a birthday scene: the one born is the eternal son, whose becoming human is related to humanity’s salvation and adoption. hopko points to galatians 4:4–7 and the feast’s confession of christ’s divine and human identity.

the meeting of the lord in the temple meeting of the lord hypapante reception of the lord feasts the meeting of the lord concerns the forty-day-old christ brought to jerusalem and recognized by simeon and the prophetess anna. hopko’s account identifies the feast with the biblical event of luke 2 and gives february 2 as its calendar date. simeon receives christ while mary and anna stand nearby. joseph carries the birds offered under the law; a canopied altar identifies the temple setting. led by the holy spirit, simeon recognizes the messiah and speaks the words now heard at orthodox vespers. he also foretells opposition to christ and sorrow for mary. anna thanks god and tells others who await jerusalem’s redemption. the published explanation places the encounter within the mosaic law: the divine lawgiver is carried as an infant and fulfills the law he gave. hopko explains the feast through this meeting with the incarnate son, not only through a recollection of the past. he connects simeon’s words with the church’s witness to salvation and identifies the light revealed to the gentiles. the infant received by simeon and the one worshiped as god are the same christ.

the theophany: baptism of christ epiphany baptism of christ manifestation of god feasts theophany depicts christ’s baptism by john in the jordan and the manifestation of the trinity. hopko distinguishes the feast’s present focus from the earlier broader epiphany celebration, which also included events surrounding christ’s birth. its printed date is january 6. christ stands in the jordan, john extends his hand toward him, and angels wait opposite. a descending ray and dove indicate the divine manifestation. hopko explains epiphany as manifestation or shining forth. in the gospel event, the father bears witness to the son and the holy spirit appears as a dove. john’s baptism therefore reveals christ as messiah and as one of the holy trinity. the source links the feast with its biblical readings and the great blessing of water, interpreting christ’s immersion in relation to the sanctification of creation. the oca explanation connects the visible event with god’s saving presence in the created world. the father’s witness is given below directly from the gospel, in the identified kjv edition. and lo a voice from heaven, saying, this is my beloved son, in whom i am well pleased.

the transfiguration metamorphosis metamorphosis of the lord feasts the mother of god parish explains this festal image as the revelation of divine glory in christ before his suffering in jerusalem. its teaching connects the light seen by the disciples with the resurrection and the promised fulfillment of god’s kingdom. christ occupies the center within a mandorla, the surrounding field of glory. moses and elijah stand beside him; peter, james, and john react below. the parish associates moses and elijah with the law and the prophets, and with the dead and the living. the selected russian icon is dated 1405 in the file description and identified with the novgorod museum. the parish’s explanation concerns the iconographic type; individual colors, mountain shapes, and the apostles’ poses vary among surviving examples. the published explanation says the vision strengthened the disciples before the humiliation of the cross. it also connects the feast with christ’s second coming and creation filled with divine light. this is the parish’s theological reading of the image. and was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.

the raising of lazarus lazarus saturday lazarus of bethany feasts st. nicholas parish places lazarus saturday immediately before holy week and pairs it with palm sunday. the published account reads the raising of christ’s friend as assurance before the passion and an anticipation of the universal resurrection. christ calls toward the tomb while lazarus emerges still wrapped in burial cloths. mary and martha bow before him. disciples and other witnesses surround the event; the removed stone and the walled city complete the explanation’s account of the composition. the selected fifteenth-century icon is identified as work of the novgorod school from the kirillo-belozersky monastery, now in the russian museum, saint petersburg. this historic panel is a different artwork from the modern icon illustrated on the parish’s page. the parish explains that christ’s tears for his friend manifest his humanity, while his command over the dead manifests divine power. its interpretation joins grief and victory rather than treating lazarus’s return simply as an isolated marvel. jesus said unto her, i am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:

the entry into jerusalem palm sunday triumphal entry feasts the mother of god parish identifies the entry into jerusalem as a great feast following the raising of lazarus. its explanation relates the entrance on a donkey to zechariah’s prophecy and to christ’s kingship as he approaches his death and resurrection. christ rides toward the walled city, accompanied by his disciples. people greet him with branches; children spread garments along his path. the parish explains these gestures as honors offered to a king and identifies hosanna as a plea for salvation. the selected panel is identified in its source as a sixteenth-century athonite icon. its composition belongs to the same festal subject discussed by the parish; specific architecture and the placement of people are features of this particular surviving example. the published explanation connects the donkey with the inclusion of the nations in the new covenant and the peace of christ’s heavenly kingdom. these are the parish article’s symbolic readings, distinct from the gospel’s narrated actions. and the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cried, saying, hosanna to the son of david: blessed is he that cometh in the name of the lord; hosanna in the highest.

the crucifixion golgotha the cross of christ scriptural scenes st. nicholas parish’s holy friday account places the crucifixion within christ’s passion, death, and burial. it explains his death through his voluntary love and obedience, and through the defeat of death that the church celebrates at pascha. the crucifixion type shows christ nailed to the cross, with his mother and other witnesses alongside. blood and water from his pierced side recall john’s gospel. the skull below refers to golgotha and, in the tradition reported by the parish, adam’s grave. the selected russian panel is attributed to dionisius and dated 1500. the parish distinguishes the crucifixion from related holy friday images: the extreme humility combines the dead christ and the tomb, while the lamentation concerns the preparation of his body for burial. these related compositions concern different moments of the passion and should not be treated as interchangeable titles for the same image. when jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, it is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.

the resurrection: descent into hades anastasis descent into hades harrowing of hell feasts the mother of god parish identifies the descent into hades as a traditional image of holy saturday and the resurrection. it explicitly presents the composition as theological depiction, rather than an eyewitness description of an event someone observed and recorded. christ stands within a mandorla above the shattered gates of hades, raising adam and receiving eve and the righteous. broken locks, bars, and chains beneath him express the destruction of death’s captivity. the source identifies adam with the human race. the selected icon from the ferapontov monastery is attributed in the file record to dionisius and his workshop. it includes a company of the righteous around christ and additional action below; the explanatory text addresses the shared type rather than cataloguing every figure. the parish reads christ’s action as deliverance from the kingdom of death. his resurrection is shown reaching the ancestral dead, while the broken gates visualize the victory proclaimed by the feast. the explanation identifies christ’s death itself with his trampling of death. for since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. for as in adam all die, even so in christ shall all be made alive.

the myrrh-bearing women at the tomb myrrhbearers ointment-bearing women women at the sepulchre scriptural scenes the published iconographic article explains the women’s name through the ointments they brought to christ’s tomb. it places their orthodox commemoration on the second sunday after pascha. their vessels identify the purpose of their visit: care for the body of jesus. the women approach carrying vessels. an angel in white points toward the empty tomb and burial cloths, announcing that christ has risen. the article describes this image as a representation of the gospel encounter, in contrast with the theological descent into hades composition. the selected vologda icon is dated by its source to the end of the fifteenth or beginning of the sixteenth century. its subject is the women’s encounter at the tomb; other images called myrrhbearers instead assemble the commemorated saints without narrating this scene. the article’s discussion of hymnography emphasizes the women’s grief, their encounter with the angel, and their commission to announce the resurrection. the focus is the empty tomb’s good news, rather than the depiction of christ emerging from it. and he saith unto them, be not affrighted: ye seek jesus of nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him.

the ascension ascension of the lord analepsis feasts the mother of god parish places the ascension on the fortieth day after pascha, a thursday. its icon explanation connects the enthroned and ascending lord with his continuing blessing, teaching, and guidance of the church. christ appears above in a mandorla, blessing with one hand and holding a scroll. below, the mother of god stands calmly in prayer between angels, while the disciples look upward and gesture. the article identifies the assembled group with the church. the selected icon is attributed to an unidentified painter of candia and dated to the second half of the fifteenth century. its published description identifies the mount of olives, the apostles, the mother of god, and angels carrying christ’s circular glory. the parish notes that paul appears in the common composition although he was not an eyewitness to the ascension. his inclusion makes the image an account of the church’s fullness and commission, rather than a photograph-like roster of the historical gathering. and when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.

pentecost: the descent of the holy spirit pentecost descent of the holy spirit feasts bishop joachim of amissos explains pentecost as the descent of the holy spirit fifty days after the resurrection. his published account relates the apostles’ languages and teaching to the church’s proclamation and the prophecy of joel. in the type he describes, the apostles sit on a curved bench beneath rays and tongues of fire. peter and paul occupy leading places. the crowned figure below personifies the world in darkness, receiving the apostles’ teaching represented by twelve scrolls. the selected historic novgorod image is titled the descent of the holy spirit in its file record. its semicircular apostolic assembly and lower crowned figure correspond to the type discussed in bishop joachim’s account; it is not the new saint nicholas shrine artwork. the bishop stresses that the composition depicts the church’s fullness rather than a photographic record: paul, mark, and luke can appear although not all belonged to the original twelve. the central place belongs to christ, the church’s head. and there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. and they were all filled with the holy ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the spirit gave them utterance.

the dormition of the mother of god dormition koimesis falling asleep of the theotokos feasts the mother of god parish’s explanation, including a feast account by fr. thomas hopko, presents the dormition as mary’s death and glorification in christ. it explicitly identifies the account as church tradition, rather than a story narrated in the canonical gospels. mary lies upon a bier among apostles, bishops, and women. christ stands above her in glory holding a white-clad child, representing her soul. the image reverses the familiar relationship of the mother of god carrying the infant christ. the selected cretan icon dates to the second half of the fifteenth century. its file description identifies additional episodes: the apostles’ arrival, mary’s translation above, and the traditional episode involving jephonias below. these additions are features of this example, not gospel eyewitness details. the published feast account gives august 15 as the church-calendar date, preceded by a two-week fast. it reads mary’s glorification as a sign of the resurrection and the eternal life promised in christ. the stated feast date is not a civil-calendar conversion. for he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.

the exaltation of the holy cross elevation of the cross universal exaltation of the precious and life-giving cross feasts holy cross parish’s published feast account commemorates the finding of christ’s cross and its elevation before the people. it gives september 14 as the church-calendar feast date; this label does not itself select a civil-calendar equivalent. the icon type shows patriarch macarius lifting the cross from the pulpit. clergy and laypeople gather around him, including saint helen; deacons carry candles. the article explains the composition through the church’s traditional narrative of the cross’s discovery in jerusalem. in the published tradition, helen finds three crosses, a healing identifies christ’s cross, and macarius raises it so the people can see. this is the feast account’s sacred narrative, distinct from the date and provenance of any surviving icon. the selected palekh icon is dated to the middle of the nineteenth century in its file record. the parish reads the feast as the transformation of an instrument of shame into a sign of victory over death. it connects the cross with the universality of redemption and the contrast between divine and worldly wisdom. for the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of god.

all saints synaxis of all saints sunday of all saints saints the orthodox church in america dedicates the sunday following pentecost to all saints, including those known only to god. its account includes apostles, martyrs, prophets, hierarchs, monastics, and righteous people, joining diverse lives through the work of the holy spirit. the selected russian icon, dated 1890, assembles many ranks of haloed saints below a heavenly register. the file description identifies the subject as all saints. this particular historical composition represents a collective gathering rather than a portrait of one named saint. the oca account cautiously proposes that the feast may have begun as a commemoration of all martyrs and later widened. it also describes the feast’s prominence in the reign of emperor leo vi and his wife, empress theophano, in the ninth century. the same account distinguishes confessors from executed martyrs: confessors suffered for their faith without being put to death. it also includes righteous people who attained holiness while living in ordinary society. the categories describe different forms of witness, not one required biography. wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,

the deesis deesis deisis supplication intercession christ fr. vladimir berzonsky describes the deesis as christ enthroned, flanked by the mother of god and saint john the baptist turning toward him in prayer. he explains its greek name through adoration, prayer, and intercession on behalf of human beings. the selected early-eighteenth-century deesis comes from the iconostasis of a chapel in the church of elijah the prophet, yaroslavl, according to its file description. the three figures occupy a single panel: christ at the center, mary and john beside him. the uffizi’s separate russian deesis object illustrates another format: three small panels probably joined as a folding traveling icon. the museum also documents variations in the figures’ posture. the title therefore names a compositional relationship that appears across more than one object format. metropolitan tikhon likewise identifies mary and john as the principal intercessors in the deesis. his published explanation calls john prophet, forerunner, and baptist, relating his place beside christ to the different aspects of his ministry. i exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men;

john the forerunner: angel of the desert john the baptist angel of the wilderness john the forerunner saints the uffizi explains the winged baptist as a messenger preparing christ’s advent. the wings belong to the iconographic title angel of the desert; the explanation relates them to biblical prophecies of the messenger and forerunner. the selected icon is attributed to prokopiy chirin of the stroganov school, dated to the 1620s, and identified with the tretyakov gallery. john stands with wings, a scroll, and a vessel; the artwork’s title identifies him as the desert angel. the museum traces the winged type’s popularity in eastern christianity to the thirteenth century. in the related uffizi example, a severed head in a basin refers to john’s martyrdom, while smaller scenes show his birth and beheading. those scenes are specific to that museum’s example. metropolitan tikhon’s reflection names john prophet, forerunner, and baptist and interprets him as the friend of the bridegroom. this published orthodox explanation concerns john’s ministry; the wings are an artistic expression of his messenger role. as it is written in the prophets, behold, i send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee. the voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare ye the way of the lord, make his paths straight.

saint nicholas the wonderworker nicholas of myra nicholas of bari nicholas the wonderworker saints the oca’s hagiographic account remembers nicholas as archbishop of myra in lycia, a compassionate pastor and wonderworker. its stories connect episcopal teaching with care for the poor, protection of the unjustly condemned, and deliverance of travelers. the selected late-fifteenth- or early-sixteenth-century icon, identified with poland in its file title, presents nicholas as a bishop holding the gospel and blessing. smaller surrounding scenes narrate his life. this narrative border distinguishes it from a simple bust portrait. the published life tells of secret gifts for three impoverished daughters, rescue of condemned men, and aid at sea. these episodes are received hagiographic traditions. the account also records the transfer of his relics to bari in 1087. the oca distinguishes russian icon types rather than reducing all nicholas images to one pattern: zaraisk shows a blessing figure with a gospel, while mozhaisk shows him holding a sword and a city. the selected panel belongs to the bishop-and-gospel visual tradition. remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of god: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.

saint george and the dragon george the victory-bearer george the great martyr saint george slaying the serpent saints the oca’s life presents george as a christian soldier who refused idolatry, suffered under diocletian, and was beheaded on april 23, 303. its title victory-bearer refers especially to his endurance in martyrdom, not simply military achievement. the selected fifteenth-century novgorod icon in the tretyakov gallery shows george on a white horse striking a serpent with his lance. his cloak and the horse’s movement distinguish this narrative image from standing portraits of the saint in armor. the oca recounts the dragon episode as a miracle story: a ruler’s daughter is delivered, the beast is overcome, and people turn to christ. this is the saint’s received hagiographic narrative; the icon does not establish a contemporary eyewitness record of a dragon. st. george parish gives symbolic readings of the dragon as satan or the persecuting emperor and of the rescued princess as the church or empress alexandra. these alternatives belong to that published explanation; they are not a claim that every painter intended identical details. greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.

saint seraphim of sarov seraphim of sarov seraphim the wonderworker saints the oca’s life identifies seraphim as the russian ascetic born prochorus moshnin in kursk. it recounts his monastic life at sarov, periods of solitude and prayer, and later ministry receiving people who sought counsel and consolation. the selected icon is dated after 1903 and tentatively associated with the seraphimo-diveevsky monastery workshop. it presents the elderly, white-bearded seraphim holding a cross. this portrait differs from narrative icons showing him praying upon a rock or with visitors. the oca’s feast account dates his glorification to 1903, seventy years after his repose, and describes the translation and public veneration of his relics during the celebrations. the account distinguishes memorial services before the glorification from the festivities that followed. in a published sermon, metropolitan hilarion relates seraphim’s long prayer in the forest and on a rock to the loving kindness that drew people to him. the account presents his example within the church’s received memory, rather than prescribing his ascetic labors to beginners. but the fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.

the jerusalem icon of the theotokos jerusalem hodegetria ierusalimskaya theotokos the jerusalem icon has a received history extending from gethsemane through constantinople and rus. the oca explicitly calls its attribution to luke a tradition. the displayed sixteenth-century hodegetria shows mary holding christ, who raises a hand in blessing. her other hand turns towards him. the work is an identified historical jerusalem-type icon; its surviving paint, frame and date belong to this particular object, not to a first-century portrait. the oca recounts transfers to constantinople in463, korsun in988, then novgorod and moscow. it connects the icon with military deliverance and prince vladimir’s gift to the newly christian novgorod community. these are the commemoration’s received historical claims, not an independently reconstructed chain of custody for every surviving copy. the account says the original was taken during the 1812 invasion and an authenticated copy replaced it in the dormition cathedral. it commemorates the icon on october 12, november 13 and the fifth saturday of lent. those printed dates and the movable observance remain distinct. the displayed sixteenth-century work is not presented as the lost original or as proof that luke painted this surviving panel.

the feodorovskaya icon of the theotokos feodorovskaya theodore–kostroma theotokos the feodorovskaya, or theodore–kostroma, icon belongs to the church’s memory of kostroma and the princely family of alexander nevsky. its traditional origin and the dating of the pictured object are separate source claims. the pictured historical panel shows the mother of god holding christ in a close embrace. its catalogue identifies the theodore icon and dates the artwork to the twelfth century. that object dating is not the same as the traditional attribution to the evangelist luke. the oca connects the icon’s name with prince yaroslav’s baptismal name theodore and follows its place in the family of alexander nevsky. it later associates the icon with the acceptance of the throne by michael romanov in 1613. its printed narrative also acknowledges differences among accounts of the icon’s history. the account also links the icon with a cathedral and a chapel dedicated to theodore stratelates at kostroma. the same account describes a two-sided icon, with saint paraskeva on the reverse, and the production of later copies with narrative border scenes. its march 14 commemoration recalls the romanov episode. these details identify a particular revered image and its reception, rather than a generic name for every tenderness icon.

the bogolyubovo icon of the mother of god bogolyubskaya bogolyubov theotokos the oca associates this russian icon with prince andrew bogolyubsky’s vision and the establishment of a church and monastery near vladimir. the selected vladimir-suzdal museum photograph identifies a twelfth-century panel. mary stands at full length with a scroll, turned toward christ in the upper corner; extensive historic surface loss remains visible. the published tradition distinguishes the icon transported by andrew, later known as the vladimir icon, from the new image commissioned to record the vision. the oca places the journey in 1155 and gives june 18 for the bogolyubov commemoration. the age and location of this selected museum panel are supplied by its own artwork record. the account says the bogolyubov image remained at the place of the vision, while the vladimir image was transferred to the city’s dormition cathedral. the two titles are therefore kept distinct. the oca’s account describes mary lifting her hand toward christ and receiving his blessing. it also records later variants with groups of saints. those details belong to the source’s account of the type; this worn historic example is not silently identified with every later moscow variant. and mary said, behold the handmaid of the lord; be it unto me according to thy word. and the angel departed from her.

the pantanassa icon of the theotokos queen of all vsetsaritsa theotokos vatopedi identifies pantanassa as a seventeenth-century portable icon in its katholikon. its published account associates the image with repentance and healing. the seventeenth-century panel presents mary and christ on an elaborate throne, with angels behind them. christ sits on her lap with one hand raised. the two angels flank the upper part of the throne. the red mantle, gold setting and upright figures belong to the displayed vatopedi composition. the local reproduction shows the historical work rather than a newly painted generic mother of god. the monastery locates the icon by the northeastern column of its main church. its account, attributed to contemporary elders, recounts a young man being thrown down by an unseen force, then acknowledging involvement in magic and changing his life. the source presents this as a miraculous event within the icon’s veneration. vatopedi also reports healings of people with cancer and stories associated with a copy brought to moscow, including children in an oncology centre. these are the monastery’s reported religious testimonies. its account specifically distinguishes the seventeenth-century vatopedi panel from the moscow copy; the later copy’s reported events belong to its own shrine history.

the axion estin (it is truly meet) icon of the theotokos it is truly meet axion estin theotokos axion estin means it is truly meet. the named athonite icon is associated with the church’s hymn to the mother of god and a traditional encounter with the archangel gabriel. the reproduced icon depicts mary holding christ within a decorated metal covering. the file identifies the named axion estin icon at karyes on mount athos. its catalogue’s traditional early dating is retained as a source claim. the oca relates that a visiting monk joins a disciple in prayer and sings the hymn’s unfamiliar opening before the older more honorable than the cherubim. he writes the words on a roof tile and is revealed as gabriel. the icon is then brought to the cathedral at karyes. these are the published miracle tradition. the narrative follows both objects separately: the icon remains on athos, while the inscribed tile is sent to constantinople as testimony to the reported encounter. the account links this image with a particular hymn and location, rather than making every icon used during that hymn the axion estin original. the selected page prints july 13 for its commemoration and also discusses later copies in russian churches. that printed date is retained without a guessed civil-calendar conversion.

the mother of god of the three hands tricherousa trojerucica troeruchitsa theotokos the three-handed icon is associated in orthodox tradition with john of damascus and the hilandar monastery on mount athos. the selected image shows the hilandar icon with its metal covering and the added silver hand. the file gives a broad eighth-to-fourteenth-century range and a traditional attribution, which is not treated as documented authorship. the oca recounts john’s severed hand being healed after prayer before the mother of god. in thanksgiving he places a silver hand on the image. the later account follows the icon through saint sava’s serbian connections to hilandar. these are the published devotional traditions, not an established date for every surviving copy. the source also recounts the image occupying hilandar’s abbot’s place after a dispute over leadership. this is the local monastery’s published tradition; it is not presented as the administrative form of every orthodox community. the source explicitly explains the additional hand as an offering, and cautions against painting mary with three anatomical arms. it gives june 28 in greek usage and july 12 in slavic usage, without converting either printed calendar date into a civil date here. his mother saith unto the servants, whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.

the gerontissa icon of the theotokos eldress gerondissa theotokos gerontissa is pantokrator monastery’s principal revered marian image. the monastery explains its name through the tradition of a dying elder who wished to receive communion. the displayed gerontissa shows the mother of god standing alone, without christ in her arms. her body and hands turn to one side. a metal revetment covers much of the figure; the face and the long vertical form remain visible. this is a specific full-length composition, not a seated mother-and-child panel. the monastery places the icon’s history near its fourteenth-century foundation but distinguishes that history from the painted appearance, which it dates to the nineteenth century. it relates a period in a well during pirate raids. its location moved from behind the altar into the main church after the event associated with the elder. in the received account, the celebrant delays while the elder is near death; the mother of god’s voice from the icon urges him to act. the elder receives communion and reposes. the monastery explicitly treats this as athonite tradition. an 1869 coloured engraving by ioannis kaldis records the standing composition with miniature scenes of the monastery, the finding in the well and the filling of empty oil jars. that dated print provides a separate historical witness to the nineteenth-century imagery.

the paramythia (consolation) icon of the theotokos consolation comfort otrada and uteshenie theotokos the paramythia, consolation or comfort icon is venerated at vatopedi on mount athos. its distinctive pose is explained in the monastery’s traditional account of a warning against pirates. this file identifies a fourteenth-century paramythia image at vatopedi. christ reaches toward mary’s face while she holds his hand and turns her head. the historical artwork’s dating and the earlier date of the traditional miracle describe different things. the oca dates the warning to january 21, 807. in its narrative the mother of god warns the abbot against opening the gates; the child raises his hand toward her lips, and she repeats the warning. the abbot takes precautions and the community is spared. the reported dialogue belongs to that church tradition. the published explanation connects the unusual movement of the figures with intercession and the remembered deliverance. it records the continuing lamp and services at vatopedi as local observance. this entry preserves that published account without composing an additional symbolic interpretation of the figures or a new devotion. paramythia is the athonite greek name. the source also prints the slavic names otrada and uteshenie for the same vatopedi tradition.

the mother of god koukouzelissa kukuzelissa koukouzelis icon theotokos the oca names the koukouzelissa after the athonite singer john koukouzelis and locates it at the great lavra. the selected file identifies a twelfth-century athonite icon. a richly worked metal covering surrounds the faces of mary and the child; the record’s date describes this image rather than proving the date of the later miracle narrative. the published life describes the former court singer’s monastic life and singing in the lavra’s choir. after an akathist, he dreams of mary encouraging him and giving him a coin. the account says that the coin was placed beneath the icon and that healings were later attributed to it and the image. the episode is identified as hagiographic tradition. the oca connects the title with the hymnographer’s memory and records october 1 and the tenth friday after pascha as commemorations. the movable reference is retained as printed, without constructing a new universal calendar rule or identifying every copy as the original. and mary said, my soul doth magnify the lord,

and my spirit hath rejoiced in god my saviour.

for he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.

for he that is mighty hath done to me great things; and holy is his name.

praise of the theotokos with the akathist laudation of the virgin pokhvala with the akathist theotokos the fifth saturday of great lent is associated in the oca’s account with the laudation of the virgin and thanksgiving for deliverance. this fourteenth-century work places the theotokos at the centre of a broad composition of small narrative scenes. the scenes form a surrounding cycle rather than a single isolated portrait. the file identifies the work as praise to the virgin with the akathist. it is an historical illustrated laudation composition, not a photograph of the particular dionysiou shrine icon. the commemoration recounts constantinople’s deliverance and the spread of the akathist to other orthodox lands. it separately associates a revered icon with a gift to dionysiou by an emperor named alexius comnenos. those shrine traditions are not transferred to this displayed russian composition. the oca’s generic description of an enthroned mother of god with prophets also does not establish that every illustrated akathist panel reproduces the same arrangement. and mary said, my soul doth magnify the lord,

and my spirit hath rejoiced in god my saviour.

for he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.

for he that is mighty hath done to me great things; and holy is his name.

the akathist of hilandar icon of the theotokos akathist-hilandar of the akathist at hilandar theotokos the hilandar akathist icon takes its name from an akathist being read during a fire in the monastery’s main church. it is one of several different icons called of the akathist. the exact artwork record names this the akathist icon of the mother of god from hilandar. mary and the child appear cheek to cheek in a tenderness composition. the historical file is catalogued as a sixteenth-century image; that description alone does not settle every question about the panel’s restoration history. the oca places the named icon on the iconostasis of hilandar’s katholikon, or main church. its short life recounts the fire of 1837 and the icon’s preservation while the hymn was being read. it prints january 12 for the commemoration. the account is a received monastery tradition rather than a modern fire investigation. the same official account explicitly distinguishes hilandar’s image from the zographou akathist icon commemorated october 10. the shared title therefore describes a devotional association, not a single object moving between all monasteries named in such stories. the actual image and its source attribution remain attached to this entry.

the mother of god of the seven arrows semistrelnaya seven swords theotokos the oca distinguishes seven arrows from the closely related softener of evil hearts by the arrangement of the swords. this nineteenth-century russian panel depicts mary without the child, with seven blades directed toward her heart and additional saints along the borders. it is a historic example of the named type, not the vologda shrine’s original image. the published account associates the type with a concealed icon near vologda, a sick man’s reported healing, and wider recognition during the 1830 cholera outbreak. these are the source’s traditional accounts. the article identifies the vologda image with saint lazarus church from 1945. that local provenance is distinguished from the nineteenth-century copy pictured in this profile. the oca describes four swords on one side and three on the other, contrasting a three-three-one arrangement in related images. it records august 13 and the sunday of all saints. and simeon blessed them, and said unto mary his mother, behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in israel; and for a sign which shall be spoken against;
