(yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,) that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.

the belynich icon of the theotokos belynichi belynichi mother of god theotokos the belynich image was venerated by both orthodox and roman catholics. the oca traces changes in custody around the mogilev district and the monastery at belynich. the selected historic panel shows mary crowned and holding the crowned child. she carries a sceptre; christ holds an orb. its bright garments and developed royal attributes belong to this eighteenth- or nineteenth-century depiction. the file identifies its museum setting at mogilev; it is not asserted to be the first image in the shrine’s history. the oca connects the icon’s catholic custody with the period following the 1596 unia and a monastery founded in 1622–1624 by lev sapega. it records the monastery’s dissolution in 1832 and the subsequent status of the church as a parish. these details describe the received institutional history of the shrine, not the individual painter or manufacture date of the displayed museum panel. the account marks april 12, 1876 with the first orthodox liturgy after the monastery’s restoration. its account of shared veneration and later orthodox custody should not be treated as an assertion that both communions endorse every theological claim about icons or church authority. the commemorative history identifies this image’s place in the devotional life of the region.

the chernigov-elets icon of the theotokos elets-chernigov chernigov spruce tree theotokos the chernigov-elets icon is linked with the tradition of an appearance in a spruce or fir tree and a monastery near chernigov. the oca distinguishes it from another yelets image with a different observance. the photographed example is a later copy of the named chernigov-elets icon. its inscription commemorates the preservation of emperor alexander ii and names pupils of the zlatopol gymnasium with the date 5 february 1880. the old painting and the modern photographer’s cc by-sa 4.0 grant are separately identified. the oca relates an appearance in 1060 and the foundation of a monastery. it follows destruction, concealment, and restoration, but expressly says the original icon’s ultimate fate is unclear. it gives alternative accounts of its movement or disappearance and identifies later copies. the account names joannicius golyatovsky and his 1676 collection of miracle narratives in its discussion of the monastery’s restoration and a later copy. its february 5 commemoration and chernigov monastery context identify this particular tradition. the account’s other yelets icon, commemorated january 11, must not be treated as an interchangeable object merely because the names sound similar. the pictured 1880 example illustrates later reception.

the chernigov-gethsemane icon of the mother of god chernigov-gethsemane chernihiv-gethsemane theotokos the oca distinguishes this image at the trinity-sergius lavra’s gethsemane skete from the earlier ilyin-chernigov icon on which it was modeled. mary and the child are crowned in this selected 1877 copy. the file identifies it with the gethsemane image and its later location at saint george’s church in ivanteyevka; the copy is not called the eighteenth-century original. the oca describes a mid-eighteenth-century image given to the lavra in 1852 and placed in the cave church of saint michael. its account identifies thekla adrianova’s reported 1869 healing and the subsequent blessing of saint innocent of moscow. these details concern the shrine’s history and published miracle tradition, not the creation date of the selected 1877 copy. the source says the original celebration followed ilyin-chernigov’s april 16 feast and was later moved to september 1, the reported day of glorification. its account emphasizes the spiritual links among the lavra, the caves, and the earlier chernigov image. and the third day there was a marriage in cana of galilee; and the mother of jesus was there:

and both jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage.

and when they wanted wine, the mother of jesus saith unto him, they have no wine.

jesus saith unto her, woman, what have i to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come.

his mother saith unto the servants, whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.

the pskov-pechersk tenderness icon of the theotokos pskov caves tenderness umilenie of pskov theotokos this pskov caves image belongs to the eleousa or tenderness type. it is distinct from the kyiv-caves svensk composition with anthony and theodosius. the displayed nineteenth-century pskov-pechersk copy places christ’s cheek against mary’s and surrounds their faces with an elaborate decorated setting. this small panel is a later object of the named tenderness type. its date is not substituted for the earlier shrine history recorded by the oca. the oca’s tradition identifies a 1521 copy of the vladimir icon and the merchants basil and theodore bringing it to the monastery during cornelius’s abbacy. it recounts healings and associates the icon with pskov’s resistance to stephen bathory in 1581 and the 1812 crisis. the received history combines public events and miracle accounts; those source genres remain explicit. the publication interprets the closeness of the faces through love between the theotokos and christ and connects that love with christ’s sacrifice. it lists may 21, june 23, august 26, october 7 and the seventh sunday of pascha as observances. these are the source’s iconological explanation and printed calendar labels, not newly composed instructions for using an image.

the murom icon of the theotokos murom-ryazan theotokos the murom icon is associated with prince constantine’s christian mission and with saint basil of ryazan. the published history connects murom and ryazan while distinguishing later copies and commemorations. this seventeenth-century example is identified in its file record as the murom mother of god. it shows the child reclining across mary’s arms and reaching toward her face. it is a historical depiction of the named type, rather than proof that the earliest revered object survives in this file. the oca describes constantine bringing the image from kiev and a hostile crowd changing its response when he approaches with the icon. a later story follows basil carrying it on a journey over water. miraculous events remain attributed to the church account. the icon thereafter becomes associated with ryazan as well as murom. the source preserves its compound name murom-ryazan, reflecting the two places in the received account. the same account notes changes and uncertainties in the commemoration’s history and compares its pose with the yakhrom icon. its resemblance to another image does not establish that the two objects or local histories are identical. the printed april 12 observance is retained without a guessed civil-date conversion.

the svensk icon of the theotokos svena svensk-pechersk mother of god of the kyiv caves theotokos the svensk composition shows the enthroned mother of god with christ between anthony and theodosius of the caves. the oca associates its veneration with bryansk. the displayed kyiv-school panel is catalogued around 1288 and belongs to the tretyakov gallery. the two caves founders stand at either side of the throne, holding texts. its old paint and damaged edges are visible. the object’s catalogue date is distinguished from the traditional attribution to alypios, who lived earlier. the received account attributes the icon to alypios and tells of its 1288 journey from kyiv to heal prince roman of chernigov. the icon is found in an oak beside the svena river; the prince regains sight and establishes a monastery. the account later describes rescue and restoration after the monastery’s closure. antonova and komova’s 2021 study explicitly examines the foundation legend as a literary and artistic source. its abstract relates the enthroned virgin to the kyiv-caves altar mosaic and identifies the founders’ figures as early surviving portraits. this scholarly treatment of the story and the actual icon is distinct from treating every element of the legend as independently documented contemporary fact.

the yaroslavl great panagia icon of the theotokos yaroslavl oranta great panagia mother of god of the incarnation theotokos the yaroslavl great panagia is a monumental medieval icon now in the tretyakov gallery. its museum title is mother of god of the incarnation, with great panagia in parentheses. it is distinct from the yaroslavl tenderness icon. mary stands frontally with hands raised in prayer. christ appears in a medallion before her and blesses with both hands; angels occupy the upper corners. the museum discusses the familiar term orans while noting that scholarly names for this particular composition have varied. the gallery dates the panel to the first quarter of the thirteenth century, perhaps around 1224. it was rediscovered at yaroslavl’s transfiguration monastery in 1919 and entered the gallery in 1930. the proposed connection with the monastery cathedral remains a probable attribution, not an established commission record. the catalogue identifies inventory 12796, a large wooden panel measuring 193.5 by 120 centimeters, painted in egg tempera. the museum’s explanation centers on the incarnation and its liturgical significance. it interprets mary’s prayerful pose in relation to the intercession of the church and discusses the child’s episcopal gesture. these are attributed museum interpretations of this object; no unsupported color code or additional symbolism is supplied.

the tolga icon of the mother of god tolgskaya theotokos the oca places the tolga icon’s traditional appearance near yaroslavl in 1314 and connects it with bishop prochorus. the selected nineteenth-century copy shows mary and the child inclining their faces toward each other. its object date belongs to the copy; it is not presented as the 1314 image from the foundation story. the published account describes a nocturnal light, a bridge across the river, and the bishop finding an icon. his forgotten staff leads companions back to the place the next morning. the story then relates the construction of a church and the later monastery. the luminous appearance and extraordinary building episode are the source’s traditional narrative. the oca associates the new church with the entrance of the theotokos and identifies august 8 as the principal commemoration, also noting july 18. the selected copy shares the title and devotional type; its individual painter is not identified by the file record. for he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.

for he that is mighty hath done to me great things; and holy is his name.

the akhtyrka icon of the theotokos akhtyr akhtyrskaya theotokos the akhtyrka tradition centres on the mother of god beside christ’s cross and the icon found by the priest basil danilov in 1739. the selected eighteenth-century image presents mary with crossed hands beside a smaller crucifixion. her covered head and the arrangement of the hands belong to this displayed example. it is a reproduction of a specific old akhtyrka-type panel; later copies need not repeat every detail of the particular original described by a commemorative article. the oca recounts the discovery in grass near the church and a series of healing stories after the icon was cleaned. it records repeated investigations, a 1751 synodal recognition and a stone church funded with empress elizabeth’s support. the church was consecrated in 1768. these are attributed events and religious testimonies within the source’s shrine history. the oca expressly notes western stylistic features in the original it describes and says that original is not the image displayed on its page. that distinction matters for copies: the uncovered head or specific prayer gesture mentioned there cannot automatically be assigned to every akhtyrka reproduction. its printed july 2 commemoration is retained without creating a civil-date conversion.

the kasperov icon of the theotokos kasperova kasperovskaya theotokos the kasperov icon belongs to the veneration of the mother of god in the kherson and odessa region. its published account names several commemorations and separates family tradition from uncertain early provenance. the file identifies this historical image as our lady of kasperova and catalogues it as seventeenth century. a richly decorated covering surrounds the faces. the photograph illustrates the named icon; its catalogue date is not a settled account of all earlier ownership. the oca also records small images of john the baptist and the great martyr tatiana beside the central mother and child. the oca discusses a traditional transylvanian origin, but also notes why the family could not establish the icon’s history. juliana kasperova inherits it in 1809. the account records a renewal of its darkened features in 1840 and later healings, followed by public veneration and processions. these remain the source’s ecclesiastical testimony. the source describes a close embrace, the child’s hand holding mary’s veil, and a scroll in his other hand. it prints october 1, april 5, bright wednesday, and june 29 among observances. bright wednesday is movable; none is converted here into an invented fixed civil anniversary.

the korsun icon of the mother of god korsunskaya cherson icon theotokos the oca records more than one transfer tradition under the korsun title, including vladimir and euphrosyne of polotsk. the selected 1867 icon has an elaborate metal covering around mary and the child. the file identifies it at the state hermitage’s winter palace church. it is this particular historic example, not a claim that every korsun image has an identical composition. one account connects a copy brought from korsun to kiev with vladimir in 988. another concerns euphrosyne’s request for an image and its journey from ephesus through korsun to polotsk, followed by association with toropets. the oca reports a traditional attribution to luke; that attribution is not presented as documented authorship for the nineteenth-century work shown here. the published history gives october 9 as the transfer commemoration and preserves the links among ephesus, korsun, polotsk, and toropets. the profile distinguishes those journeys from the selected museum object’s own provenance, and does not combine differently named copies into one continuously documented panel. and it came to pass, that, when elisabeth heard the salutation of mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and elisabeth was filled with the holy ghost:

and she spake out with a loud voice, and said, blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.

and whence is this to me, that the mother of my lord should come to me?

for, lo, as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in mine ears, the babe leaped in my womb for joy.

and blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the lord.

the unfading flower icon of the theotokos unfading blossom unfading rose neuvyadaemy tsvet theotokos the oca explains the unfading flower title through marian imagery of purity and virginity. surviving compositions vary in the flowers, regalia and placement of the child. tikhon filatyev’s 1691 panel shows the crowned mother and child amid abundant flowers, architectural forms and royal ornament. the displayed object’s rich floral arrangement is more elaborate than a simple portrait holding a single lily. its named artist and date identify this particular work, not the earliest origin of every icon bearing the title. the oca’s described form has mary holding christ and a bouquet of white lilies. the article connects those lilies with a published marian hymn. its explanation is attributed to the issuing church; the app does not invent a meaning for each flower painted by filatyev or assume that all variants share an identical botanical arrangement. the publication lists examples in moscow, kungur, kadome, voronezh and budishch. it records an april 3 gathering at budishch and reported healings, alongside a copy of the vladimir icon. such place-specific commemorations and miracle traditions distinguish the history of an individual shrine from the broader floral title and from a museum panel dated 1691.

the burning bush icon of the theotokos unburnt bush neopalimaya kupina theotokos the burning or unburnt bush icon connects the vision of moses with the church’s confession of the incarnation. the oca explains both an older narrative form and a later star-shaped composition. this early-eighteenth-century example depicts moses beside the bush, with the mother of god and child above. it illustrates the narrative form of the subject. the source record identifies an old icon; the photograph is used complete and unchanged. the oca names the bush that burns without being consumed as an old testament prefiguration of the virgin’s childbearing. it also describes a later composition combining red and green quadrangles, prophetic scenes, angels, and the central mother and child. that description should be read as a type with variants, rather than a list of features visible in every example. now moses kept the flock of jethro his father in law, the priest of midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of god, even to horeb.

and the angel of the lord appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.

and moses said, i will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.

and when the lord saw that he turned aside to see, god called unto him out of the midst of the bush, and said, moses, moses. and he said, here am i.

and he said, draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.

moreover he said, i am the god of thy father, the god of abraham, the god of isaac, and the god of jacob. and moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon god.

the mother of god, seeker of the lost seeker of the perishing recovery of the perishing vzyskanie pogibshikh theotokos the oca explains this title as referring to people in danger of spiritual death as well as bodily peril. the selected seventeenth-century image identifies the seeker of the perishing. mary and the child occupy the central composition, with small standing saints along its borders. its date does not establish the origin of every wonderworking icon bearing the title. the source explicitly says reliable accounts of the type’s origin are lacking. it recounts several separate wonderworking images, including theodotos obukhov’s rescue in a blizzard and a commissioned copy at bor. it also follows a moscow image damaged during the 1812 invasion. these are distinct traditions, not one securely documented object history. the oca also mentions a moscow orphanage church dedicated to this title in 1835, showing its reception beyond a single local wonderworking image. the oca supplies the russian and greek forms of the title and preserves several english translations. the name is therefore treated as a devotional title shared by multiple images, rather than evidence that every copy has the same painter or shrine history. for the son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.

the surety of sinners icon of the theotokos sporuchnitsa greshnykh odrino surety of sinners theotokos the surety of sinners title comes from the icon’s inscription. the oca explains its unusual handclasp as a gesture of surety. the displayed nineteenth-century panel shows crowned mary and christ with their hands joined. the figures appear within a curved ornamental border and an inscription. its historical date and surviving visual form identify a particular copy; they do not establish the unknown original painter or date discussed in the ecclesiastical history. the oca states that the original date and painter are unknown. it locates the icon’s nineteenth-century veneration at saint nicholas odrino monastery and records its removal from a neglected chapel after dreams in 1843, followed by healing accounts. the article also describes a copy made in 1848 and later donated to saint nicholas at khamovniki. the source reads the child’s grasp of mary’s thumb and small finger in relation to the inscription and connects the type with an akathist to the protection of the theotokos. those explanations are the publication’s account of the composition. it gives additional observances on may 29 and the thursday of all saints week; the days concern this icon’s commemoration, not a rule assembled for private worship.

the deliverer icon of the theotokos deliveress izbavitelnitsa theotokos the deliverer icon is associated with mount athos, the monk martinian, and the later monastery of new athos. its published history contains reports of deliverance from calamity and healing. this named deliveress image is catalogued as nineteenth century. mary holds the blessing child, surrounded by a metal covering and devotional ornament. it is a later historical representation of the named icon, not an assertion that the photographed surface was painted by an apostle. the oca follows the icon from constantine theodoulos to his disciple martinian. in 1841 martinian brings it to the region of sparta, where the narrative recounts deliverance from locusts and healings. he later returns to athos. the account ultimately places the icon at new athos after its transfer in 1889. the account gives martinian’s repose in 1884 and names archimandrite makarios in the later transfer to the caucasus. these dates belong to the published itinerary. the title deliverer identifies the published tradition of help in danger. the reported miracles and local history remain attributed to that ecclesiastical account. this page does not treat the picture as an independently acting power or add a new prayer formula to the source’s record.

christ the great high priest megas archiereus great hierophant king of kings christ the selected late-sixteenth-century candia icon presents christ enthroned in episcopal and imperial garments. its title is the great high priest. christ wears a sakkos, omophorion, and imperial crown, with kneeling donors beside the throne. the greek file description identifies john 18:36 and matthew 26:26 among the gospel passages shown in the open book. the file dates this panel to the late sixteenth century and identifies an unknown painter of candia. the visible donors belong to this particular surviving work; they are not treated as obligatory features of every great high priest icon. seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, jesus the son of god, let us hold fast our profession.

for we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.

let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. but this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood.

the multiplication of the loaves feeding of the five thousand scriptural scenes the multiplication of the loaves depicts christ feeding the multitude with five loaves and two fish. the selected reading is matthew’s account of the five thousand, keeping it distinct from the separate feeding of four thousand. the illustration is a sixth-century mosaic at sant’apollinare nuovo in ravenna. christ stands centrally while attendants present bread and fish. its source specifically identifies the feeding of the multitude. the work is an ancient wall mosaic, not a recent icon painting. matthew describes compassion for the crowd, the disciples’ concern about food, christ’s blessing and breaking of the loaves, distribution through the disciples, and twelve baskets of remaining fragments. the number and sequence belong to this account; no additional symbolic meaning is assigned to every visible basket. and jesus went forth, and saw a great multitude, and was moved with compassion toward them, and he healed their sick.

christ the good shepherd the shepherd with the sheep scriptural scenes a young shepherd carries a sheep on his shoulders between other sheep. this is an early roman christian fresco reproduced in a 1903 publication. the central figure holds the animal across his shoulders, with a vessel hanging from one hand. two sheep stand below within the painted roundel. the scene uses a pastoral figure rather than the later frontal, bearded pantocrator format. the file describes a third-century roman catacomb painting reproduced in joseph wilpert’s 1903 die malereien der katakomben roms. its filename and description differ about the specific catacomb, so the exact burial site is not treated as established here. the dated historical reproduction and the ancient pastoral subject remain identified. i am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.

christ the true vine the vine and the branches scriptural scenes christ the true vine gives visual form to the language of john 15. the displayed icon gathers christ, the apostles, and branches into one composition; its theme is distinguished from later winepress images with a related title. the selected image is a sixteenth-century icon catalogued at athens. christ appears in the vine with the apostles among its branches. the catalogue identifies the true vine subject; the composition is preserved complete, with its inscriptions and surrounding figures. this is a historical painted interpretation of a scriptural image, rather than an illustration of a literal tree mentioned at a particular place in the gospel narrative. its sixteenth-century dating belongs to the specific object record. other works titled true vine may have different compositions and should be identified individually. i am the true vine, and my father is the husbandman.

if ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you.

herein is my father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples.

the communion of the apostles eucharistic communion of the apostles communion with bread scriptural scenes the selected fifteenth-century panel is catalogued as the eucharist with bread. it belongs to the trinity cathedral iconostasis at sergiev posad. christ gives communion to approaching apostles beside an altar-like table. this is the bread-communion panel, distinct from its wine companion and from the narrative last supper around a dining table. the source attributes it to the daniel chorny and andrey rublev workshop. for i have received of the lord that which also i delivered unto you, that the lord jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread:

peter and paul the chief apostles peter and paul of belozersk saints the belozersk icon places peter and paul side by side as full-length figures. the old panel is identified with the novgorod school. both apostles hold books or scrolls and turn slightly towards the centre. the contrasting hair, beard and garments distinguish the paired figures. their halos and inscriptions identify them within the named historical work; this is not a group portrait of the entire apostolic company. the file dates the work to the twelfth–thirteenth centuries and locates its provenance at belozersk. this object history is distinct from the apostles’ first-century lives. the readings below preserve separate gospel and pauline voices instead of combining their words into one invented speech. he saith unto them, but whom say ye that i am?

and i will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. for i am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.

i have fought a good fight, i have finished my course, i have kept the faith:

henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.

andrew the first-called andrew the first-called apostle saints andrew the first-called is identified in the greek church reading as peter’s brother from bethsaida and a former disciple of john the baptist. his icon is therefore distinct from those of andrew of crete or other saints named andrew. the displayed historical icon comes from saint paraskevi’s church at langadas. its catalogue identifies the apostle andrew and dates it before the twentieth century. he is shown as an aged apostle holding a scroll; the file’s named subject distinguishes him from homonymous saints. goarch explains the title first-called through andrew’s response to john the baptist’s witness and his following of christ. it later recounts missionary work and crucifixion at patras, associating the x-shaped cross with his memory. the martyrdom detail is a church tradition beyond the gospel reading below. one of the two which heard john speak, and followed him, was andrew, simon peter’s brother.

he first findeth his own brother simon, and saith unto him, we have found the messias, which is, being interpreted, the christ.

and he brought him to jesus. and when jesus beheld him, he said, thou art simon the son of jona: thou shalt be called cephas, which is by interpretation, a stone.

the three holy hierarchs basil, gregory, and john synaxis of the three hierarchs saints the three holy hierarchs icon joins basil the great, gregory the theologian, and john chrysostom. their common feast emphasizes concord in teaching rather than rivalry among their admirers. the selected icon is catalogued as a seventeenth- or eighteenth-century image of the synaxis of the three holy hierarchs. all three appear in episcopal vestments with gospel books or scrolls. their common presentation identifies this synaxis rather than an assembly of three unnamed bishops. the oca places the origin of their common observance in disputes among christians at constantinople who preferred one teacher over another. its narrative recounts their appearance to john of euchaita and the establishment of january 30 as a shared commemoration. the vision remains attributed to that ecclesiastical tradition. the published account says the three reject factional rivalry and affirm their equality before god. their combined icon accordingly belongs to a particular commemorated synaxis. it does not turn distinct biographies, writings, or historical settings into one anonymous author; readers can study the named teachers separately alongside the common image. their common feast therefore supplements the study of each teacher rather than replacing his separate commemoration, name, and body of writings.

basil the great basil of caesarea basil the hierarch saints the selected fifteenth-century novgorod icon of basil is held by norway’s national museum of art, architecture and design. it is a full-length historic hierarch portrait. basil wears a cross-patterned episcopal omophorion and holds a book. the narrow panel preserves the whole figure. these are visible attributes of this selected work; the profile does not infer a specific liturgical action from his pose. wace’s historical dictionary identifies basil as bishop of caesarea in cappadocia and connects his family with macrina, gregory of nyssa, and peter. its biography is an authored historical assessment; basil’s own words are supplied separately below. through the holy spirit comes our restoration to paradise, our ascension into the kingdom of heaven, our return to the adoption of sons, our liberty to call god our father, our being made partakers of the grace of christ, our being called children of light, our sharing in eternal glory, and, in a word, our being brought into a state of all "fulness of blessing," both in this world and in the world to come, of all the good gifts that are in store for us, by promise hereof, through faith, beholding the reflection of their grace as though they were already present, we await the full enjoyment.

john chrysostom john the golden-mouthed saints dionisius presents john chrysostom as a bishop in a narrow, full-length icon. he holds a gospel book and wears a light vestment with dark crosses. the bishop’s head inclines and one hand is raised while the other supports the book. the long figure and simple background focus the composition on the identified hierarch. this is dionisius’s historical depiction, not a portrait claimed to have been painted during john’s lifetime. the file identifies dionisius as the artist. its provenance is retained with the original local image and source record. the historical reference excerpt below discusses john’s scriptural interpretation from a named early-twentieth-century catholic author; its critical terminology is not presented as an orthodox synodal definition. as an exegete chrysostom is of the highest importance, for he is the chief and almost the only successful representative of the exegetical principles of the school of antioch. diodorus of tarsus had initiated him into the grammatico-historical method of that school, which was in strong opposition to the eccentric, allegorical, and mystical interpretation of origen and the alexandrian school. but chrysostom rightly avoided pushing his principles to that extreme to which, later on, his friend theodore of mopsuestia, the teacher of nestorius, carried them. he did not even exclude all allegorical or mystical explanations, but confined them to the cases in which the inspired author himself suggests this meaning.

gregory the theologian gregory of nazianzus saints gregory the theologian is the cappadocian bishop and teacher associated with constantinople and the confession of the trinity. he is not gregory of nyssa, gregory palamas, or gregory the dialogist. the illustrated russian icon is catalogued as sixteenth century and explicitly identifies gregory of nazianzus. his episcopal vestments, raised hand, and book belong to this historical depiction; their presence alone would not identify an otherwise unnamed bishop. the greek church reading follows gregory’s friendship with basil and his theological preaching in constantinople. it connects his title theologian with the depth of his teaching about the trinity. the primary passage below is his own theological oration in a named public-domain translation. xiv. what is our quarrel and dispute with both? to us there is one god, for the godhead is one, and all that proceedeth from him is referred to one, though we believe in three persons. for one is not more and another less god; nor is one before and another after; nor are they divided in will or parted in power; nor can you find here any of the qualities of divisible things; but the godhead is, to speak concisely, undivided in separate persons; and there is one mingling of light, as it were of three suns joined to each other. when then we look at the godhead, or the first cause, or the monarchia, that which we conceive is one; but when we look at the persons in whom the godhead dwells, and at those who timelessly and with equal glory have their being from the first cause--there are three whom we worship.

spyridon of trimythous spiridon spyridon of cyprus saints the selected icon of spyridon from gorno statitsa is dated 1720 in its file record. the whole historic portrait is retained. spyridon is shown as a bishop, with his characteristic rounded cap, liturgical vestments, and a book. the date and location identify this particular icon rather than an apostolic-age likeness. spyridon, bp. of trimithus in cyprus, one of the most popularly celebrated of the bishops attending the council of nicaea, although his name is not found in the list of signatures. he was the centre of many legendary stories which socrates heard from his fellow-islanders (socr. h. e. i. 12). spyridon was married, with at least one daughter, irene. he continued his occupation as a sheep farmer after, for his many virtues, he had been called to the episcopate. he is mentioned by athanasius among the orthodox bishops at the council of sardica (athan. apol. ii. p. 768). his body was first buried in his native island, then removed to constantinople, and when the turks captured the city it was transmitted to corfu, where it is annually carried in procession round the capital as the patron saint of the ionian isles (stanley, eastern church, p. 126). i am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.

panteleimon the healer pantaleon panteleemon saints the fifteenth-century byzantine panel depicts the young physician martyr panteleimon. its catalogue identifies the pushkin museum work. panteleimon stands in a red garment with a small medical container and a slender instrument. his youthful face and compact pose are preserved within the worn panel. these visible attributes identify the traditional physician depiction without establishing every detail of his later martyrdom narratives. the underlying painting is identified as a fifteenth-century byzantine work. the file-level reproduction carries a cc by-sa3.0 record and retains its exact attribution. the object’s medieval date is distinct from the martyr’s life in the early fourth century. martyr, died about 305. according to legend he was the son of a rich pagan, eustorgius of nicomedia, and had been instructed in christianity by his christian mother, eubula. afterwards he became estranged from christianity. he studied medicine and became physician to the emperor maximianus. he was won back to christianity by the priest hermolaus. upon the death of his father he came into possession of a large fortune. envious colleagues denounced him to the emperor during the diocletian persecution. … … it was not until he himself desired it that it was possible to behead him.

demetrius of thessalonica demetrios the myrrh-streamer saints demetrius of thessalonica is remembered as a great martyr and protector of the city. the greek feast account joins his public rank with a confession of christ that takes priority over imperial favor. this fresco in the protaton church on mount athos is attributed to manuel panselinos and dated around 1290–1310 by the object record. demetrius appears in military dress. the artwork illustrates the traditional military-saint iconography without making every armed haloed figure demetrius. the published life describes his preaching and the conversion of others despite persecution. its martyrdom account says soldiers pierce him with lances in prison after nestor’s victory. these details identify the received thessalonian narrative and distinguish his death from the dragon-slaying story associated with george. the greek account places his suffering under galerius maximian, around 306, and names thessalonica as the setting of his confession. goarch calls him myrrh-streamer and records the continuing ecclesiastical commemoration. the title belongs to the saint’s veneration and relic tradition. the source’s reported miracles remain attributed; the painting’s military clothing does not function here as a new instruction about warfare or as a generalized symbolic code.

barbara the great martyr barbara of heliopolis saints the nineteenth-century kastoria icon presents barbara as a young crowned martyr. the image comes from the named saint barbara church. barbara wears richly patterned garments and holds a cross. the painted figure survives within a larger church setting rather than an invented new portrait. the file’s date and location describe this particular kastoria depiction; they are not treated as the date or place of her martyrdom. the source identifies a nineteenth-century icon at saint barbara church in kastoria. the historical reference passage below preserves a received account of dioscorus, the tower and the three windows. its author’s distinction between later narrative and early evidence remains part of the reading’s bibliographic context. … according to these narratives, which are essentially the same, barbara was the daughter of a rich heathen named dioscorus. she was carefully guarded by her father who kept her shut up in a tower in order to preserve her from the outside world. an offer of marriage which was received through him she rejected. before going on a journey her father commanded that a bath-house be erected for her use near her dwelling, and during his absence barbara had three windows put in it, as a symbol of the holy trinity, instead of the two originally intended. … … when her father returned she acknowledged herself to be a christian; upon this she was ill-treated by him and dragged before the prefect of the province, martinianus, who had her cruelly tortured and finally condemned her to death by beheading. the father himself carried out the death-sentence, but in punishment for this he was struck by lightning on the way home and his body consumed. another christian named juliana suffered the death of a martyr along with barbara. …

mary of egypt mary the egyptian saints mary of egypt is remembered for repentance and long desert ascetic life. the greek reading names her encounter with zosimas and attributes the written life to sophronius of jerusalem. the pictured russian work is catalogued, with a question mark, as nineteenth century. it identifies mary of egypt in prayer, with a heavenly appearance of the mother of god and child. the uncertain artwork dating is retained rather than turned into a precise creation year. the published life follows her from alexandria to jerusalem, her inability to enter the church at the exaltation of the cross, and her resolve to repent. she crosses the jordan and lives in the wilderness. zosimas later hears her account and brings her communion; when he returns again, he finds her dead. the reading describes forty-seven years in the wilderness before its concluding encounter and testimony through zosimas. the account itself prints several proposed years of death, so this icon entry does not impose one exact chronology. it also names the fifth sunday of lent alongside april 1. her image belongs to that ecclesiastical memory of repentance, with the particular painted example distinguished from the older written narrative.

sergius of radonezh sergii of radonezh sergius with scenes from his life saints the selected seventeenth-century yaroslavl icon places sergius at the center of a surrounding life cycle. it is a historic vita icon, not a claim that the painter witnessed the episodes. sergius stands in monastic clothing with a cross above, while small scenes occupy the borders. the file identifies the yaroslavl museum example. each small episode belongs to a painted hagiographic cycle rather than a dated documentary photograph. prelates and princes applied to sergius not only for the sake of his spiritual instructions, but also to receive from him teachers, who had been trained to perfection by his converse in solitude, and who in their turn might be capable of influencing others by their good example : for from the appearance of sergius there began among us, as it were, a second era and development of monasticism; and in the ful- ness of its light our unhappy country, which had been suffering so long under the plague of the tartars, revived. take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for i am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
